chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Hammad, from Hariz, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the man who prays and does not know whether he has prayed one or two [rak'at]. He (peace be upon him) said: 'He should face [the qibla] until he is convinced that he has completed [the prayer], and this applies to Friday [prayer], and to Maghrib, and to the prayer during the journey.'
ai.seo_question: What should a Muslim do if they are unsure whether they prayed one or two rak'ats?
ai.summary: This hadith establishes the principle of *istishab* (presumption of continuity) in cases of doubt (*shakk*) during prayer, instructing the worshipper to remain in their current state until certainty is achieved. It specifically applies this ruling to prayers with variable rak'at counts, such as Friday, Maghrib, and travel prayers, reflecting the Shia juristic preference for stability over reconstruction in ambiguous situations.

en.hubeali: Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, from Hammad, from Hareyz, from Muhammad Bin Muslim who said,

‘I asked Abu Abdullahasws about the man who prays a Salāt and he does not know whether he has prayed one or two (Rak’at). Heasws said: ‘He should re-commence until he is convinced that he has completed – and in the Friday (Salāt), and in Al-Maghrib, and in the Salāt during the journey’.
en.sarwar: 2. Ali ibn Ibrahim has narrated from his father from Hammad, from Hariz from Muhammad ibn Muslim who has said the following: “

I once asked abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, about a man who performs Salah (prayer) but does not know if he has performed one or two (Rak‘at). He (the Imam) said, ‘He performs it again to ascertain that he has completed it and so also is the case with Friday, al-Maghrib and Salah (prayer) on a journey.’”
